promptText: A process is isolated with its own memory, while threads inside a process share memory. What specific danger does this shared memory introduce that isolated processes do not have?
options: Race conditions and visibility problems, because multiple threads can read and write the same heap objects concurrently with no isolation boundary between them
Threads cannot communicate with each other at all, unlike processes which use pipes or sockets
Threads require their own dedicated CPU core, unlike processes which can share one
Shared memory makes context switching between threads slower than between processes
explanation: The same shared heap that makes threads efficient (cheap communication, no IPC needed) is exactly what creates the risk of concurrent bugs like race conditions and stale-value visibility issues -- isolated processes avoid this class of bug entirely because they don't share memory, but pay for it with slower, explicit inter-process communication; thread context switches are actually faster than process switches, not slower.

promptText: Calling `thread.run()` directly versus `thread.start()` looks similar but behaves very differently. What actually happens with each, and what happens if you call `start()` twice on the same Thread object?
options: run() executes synchronously on the calling thread with no new thread created; start() creates a genuinely new thread; calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException because a thread cannot be restarted once it has run
run() and start() are functionally identical in every Java version since Java 5
start() executes synchronously like a normal method call, while run() is the one that spawns a new thread
Calling start() twice silently creates two independent threads with no error
explanation: run() is just an ordinary method call with no concurrency at all; start() is the only path to true parallel execution because it asks the JVM to register a new thread and invoke run() on it -- and because a Thread object cannot transition back to NEW once it has started, a second start() call throws IllegalThreadStateException rather than silently succeeding.

promptText: A background worker loop checks a plain (non-volatile) boolean `running` flag to decide when to stop, while another thread sets `running = false`. Why might the worker loop never actually observe the change and run forever?
options: Each thread may cache the field in a CPU register or core-local cache without volatile, so a write by one thread is not guaranteed to become visible to the other thread that only reads it
Boolean fields cannot be safely shared between threads under any circumstances, volatile or not
The worker loop will always see the update within a few nanoseconds regardless of volatile, since booleans are a single bit
Only int and long fields require volatile for visibility; boolean fields are always visible immediately
explanation: Without volatile, there is no guarantee the writing thread's update to `running` is flushed to main memory in a way the reading thread will observe, so the loop can spin forever on a stale cached value -- marking the flag volatile guarantees the write becomes visible to other threads and prevents this exact class of bug, which is its most common real-world use case.

promptText: Callable was introduced to address two specific limitations of Runnable. What are they?
options: Runnable's run() cannot return a value and cannot throw a checked exception; Callable's call() can do both, which is why Callable is used with a Future to retrieve a computed result or observe a failure
Runnable cannot be submitted to an ExecutorService at all, while only Callable can
Runnable can only be used with the deprecated Thread class, never with thread pools
Callable executes on multiple threads simultaneously, while Runnable is always confined to a single thread
explanation: run() has a void, no-throws signature, making it suitable only for fire-and-forget side effects; call() returns a value and is allowed to throw checked exceptions, so it's the right choice whenever the caller needs the result of the work or wants to observe an exception through the returned Future -- both Runnable and Callable are equally submittable to an ExecutorService.

promptText: Thread 1 holds Lock A and is waiting for Lock B; Thread 2 holds Lock B and is waiting for Lock A. What is this situation called, and what happens to both threads?
options: Deadlock -- both threads are permanently blocked because neither will release what it holds until it acquires the resource the other is holding
Livelock -- both threads keep retrying and changing state but never actually block
Starvation -- both threads eventually get access, just much later than expected
Race condition -- both threads corrupt each other's data but neither actually stops running
explanation: This circular hold-and-wait pattern is the textbook definition of deadlock: each thread is completely blocked indefinitely, unlike livelock (where threads stay active but still make no progress) or starvation (where a thread is repeatedly denied a resource but the rest of the system keeps functioning).

promptText: Why are immutable objects like String and records inherently thread safe without any synchronization?
options: Their state is fixed at construction and can never change afterward, so there is no write for concurrent threads to race on or corrupt -- every thread that reads the object always sees the same consistent value
The JVM automatically places every immutable object behind an internal monitor lock
Immutable objects can only ever be referenced by a single thread; the compiler enforces this restriction
Immutability guarantees the object will be garbage collected before a second thread can access it
explanation: Thread-safety hazards come specifically from shared MUTABLE state; because an immutable object's fields are set once and never modified, there is no possible interleaving of reads and writes that could corrupt it, so it can be freely shared across any number of threads with zero synchronization overhead -- no locking, no restriction, and no special GC treatment is involved.

promptText: A thread is WAITING versus a thread is BLOCKED are both non-running states, but they arise from different causes. What is the key distinction?
options: WAITING is a voluntary, self-induced suspension (e.g. calling wait() or join()) that resumes only when another thread signals it; BLOCKED is involuntary contention where the thread wants to enter a synchronized region but another thread currently holds that monitor
WAITING threads consume CPU cycles while spinning, whereas BLOCKED threads consume none
A BLOCKED thread can never recover and must be manually killed by the JVM
WAITING only applies to threads created via ExecutorService, while BLOCKED only applies to threads created via new Thread()
explanation: The distinguishing factor is whether the thread chose to pause itself: a WAITING thread is cooperatively suspended and will resume once notified, while a BLOCKED thread is stuck purely because it's contending for a lock someone else holds -- both states let go of the CPU rather than spin, and both are perfectly recoverable once their condition is met.

promptText: Both sleep() and wait() pause a thread, but only one releases the monitor lock it holds. Which one, and why does this matter for a thread inside a synchronized block that needs another thread to change shared state before it can continue?
options: wait() releases the lock so other threads can enter the synchronized block and change the state being waited on, then re-acquires the lock upon waking; sleep() holds onto any lock it has for the entire pause, which would deadlock a producer-consumer pattern if used instead of wait()
sleep() releases the lock while wait() holds it, so wait() is the wrong choice inside a synchronized block
Neither method releases any lock; both simply pause the thread's instruction pointer
Both methods release the lock identically; the only difference is that sleep() takes a duration argument
explanation: If a thread inside a synchronized block called sleep() while waiting for another thread to change the guarded condition, no other thread could ever enter that block to make the needed change, causing a permanent deadlock; wait() is specifically designed to release the monitor during the pause so the required state change can actually happen, then reclaims the lock before continuing.

promptText: Multiple threads are waiting on the same monitor, but each for a different condition. Why can using notify() instead of notifyAll() here cause a permanent "lost wakeup," and how does notifyAll() combined with a while-loop guard fix it?
options: notify() wakes only one arbitrary waiting thread, which might not be the one whose condition is now true, leaving the correct thread asleep forever; notifyAll() wakes every waiter so each can re-check its own condition in a while loop and only proceed if it's actually satisfied
notify() always wakes the thread with the highest priority, which guarantees correctness as long as priorities are set properly
notifyAll() is slower than notify() but otherwise behaves identically, waking exactly one thread chosen at random
Using an if statement instead of a while loop around the wait() call has no effect on correctness, only on code style
explanation: notify() picks an arbitrary waiter with no regard for which condition is now satisfied, so it can wake a thread waiting for something unrelated while the thread that should have proceeded stays asleep indefinitely; notifyAll() sidesteps this by waking everyone, but that only works correctly if each thread re-verifies its condition in a while loop (since an if would proceed even if the condition isn't actually met yet).

promptText: `AtomicInteger` is described as thread safe without using locks. What mechanism does it actually rely on internally, and what happens when two threads race to update it at the same instant?
options: It holds a volatile int and updates it via compare-and-swap (CAS): each update reads the current value, computes a new one, and atomically swaps it in only if the value hasn't changed since the read; if another thread updated it first, the operation retries in a loop rather than corrupting the value
It acquires the object's intrinsic monitor lock exactly like a synchronized method, just with a friendlier API
It queues all updates from every thread and applies them one at a time in the order threads called the method, using a background thread
It uses a ReentrantLock internally, configured in fair mode by default
explanation: AtomicInteger achieves atomicity without blocking by using CAS: a losing thread's swap simply fails and it retries with a fresh read, rather than corrupting state the way a naive count++ would -- this is fundamentally different from synchronized/ReentrantLock, which block contending threads rather than retrying in a loop.

promptText: Method A acquires a lock and then calls Method B, which acquires that same lock again on the same thread. Why doesn't this deadlock the thread against itself when using `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`?
options: Both are reentrant locks: they maintain a hold count that increments on each acquisition by the owning thread and decrements on release, so a thread already holding the lock can re-acquire it without blocking; the lock is only truly freed once the count returns to zero
Java automatically detects self-deadlock and skips the second lock acquisition silently
This scenario is only safe with ReentrantLock; the equivalent code using synchronized would deadlock the thread against itself
The second acquisition succeeds only because Method B runs on a separate thread from Method A
explanation: Reentrancy is essential whenever a locked method calls another method that needs the same lock, such as recursion or one guarded method delegating to another; without it a thread would block waiting for a lock it already owns -- and this reentrant behavior applies equally to Java's intrinsic synchronized locks and to ReentrantLock, not just the latter.

promptText: An exception is thrown inside a task submitted via `executorService.submit(callable)`, versus the same exception thrown inside a task passed to `executorService.execute(runnable)`. How does the exception surface differently in each case?
options: With submit(), the exception is captured inside the returned Future and stays silent until you call future.get(), which rethrows it wrapped in an ExecutionException; with execute(), the uncaught exception propagates immediately to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler
Both methods always print the exception to standard error immediately regardless of whether get() is called
submit() cannot be used with tasks that might throw an exception; only execute() supports exception-throwing tasks
execute() silently swallows all exceptions with no way to observe them, while submit() always terminates the JVM
explanation: This is a common source of silently swallowed errors in production: a submit()'d task's exception sits dormant inside the Future doing nothing until someone calls get() (or join()), whereas execute()'s fire-and-forget model surfaces the exception right away via the thread's uncaught exception handler -- forgetting to call get() on a submitted task can hide real failures indefinitely.

promptText: In naive CAS-based lock-free code, a thread reads a shared reference as A, computes a new value, then performs `compareAndSwap(A, newValue)`. Between the read and the swap, another thread changes the value from A to B and then back to A. Why does the CAS succeed even though the underlying state may have meaningfully changed, and how does AtomicStampedReference fix it?
options: Plain CAS only checks that the current value still equals the expected value A, so it cannot detect that it changed and changed back (the ABA problem); AtomicStampedReference pairs the value with an incrementing stamp so CAS also compares the stamp, which will have advanced even though the value itself returned to A
CAS inherently detects any intermediate change to a value, so this scenario is actually impossible with a correctly implemented CAS instruction
AtomicStampedReference solves this by making the read and the swap execute on two separate dedicated threads to avoid interference
The ABA problem only occurs with AtomicLong, never with AtomicReference or AtomicStampedReference's own internal fields
explanation: This is dangerous specifically in structures like lock-free stacks, where a node could be popped, freed, and a new node coincidentally reallocated at the same reference, fooling a CAS that only checks value equality; attaching a monotonically increasing stamp means even a value that cycles back to its original state carries an unmistakable trace that something happened in between, which the stamped CAS will detect and reject.

promptText: All four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur. Why does enforcing a consistent global lock-acquisition order across all threads prevent deadlock without needing to change the other three conditions?
options: A fixed global ordering makes a circular wait mathematically impossible -- if every thread always acquires locks in the same relative order, there can never be a cycle of threads each waiting on the next, even though mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, and no preemption remain fully in effect
Lock ordering actually eliminates mutual exclusion by allowing multiple threads to hold the same lock simultaneously as long as they acquired it in order
Lock ordering works by forcing the JVM to preempt and forcibly release locks from lower-priority threads, breaking the no-preemption condition instead of circular wait
Consistent lock ordering has no theoretical effect on deadlock; it only reduces how long threads spend blocked, without preventing it entirely
explanation: Breaking just one of the four necessary conditions is sufficient to prevent deadlock entirely, and circular wait is usually the easiest one to target in real code: if Thread 1 must always acquire Lock A before Lock B, and Thread 2 follows that same rule, neither thread can ever end up waiting on a lock held by a thread that is itself waiting on a lock the first thread holds -- the other three conditions can remain true with no ill effect.

promptText: Two naive deadlock-avoidance routines each detect lock contention and release their held lock to retry, but they keep doing this in lockstep against each other forever. Is this a deadlock, and what typically fixes it?
options: This is a livelock, not a deadlock -- the threads remain active and keep changing state (release-and-retry) in direct response to each other, so nothing is technically blocked, but no progress is ever made; introducing randomized backoff before retrying breaks the lockstep symmetry so one thread eventually proceeds
This is a deadlock, because the threads are permanently unable to acquire both locks simultaneously
This is starvation, because one thread is being denied CPU time by a higher-priority thread
This scenario is impossible in Java because ReentrantLock automatically detects and resolves lockstep retry loops
explanation: The threads here are busy and responsive -- the opposite of a deadlock's total standstill -- but their symmetric release-and-retry pattern means neither ever gets ahead, which is the definition of livelock; because the problem is the perfectly synchronized timing, adding a small random delay before each retry desynchronizes the threads enough that one of them wins the race and makes progress.
